segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If I speak in the tongues of people and of angels but do not have love, I have become resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if I have the gift of prophecy and understand all the mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if I dole out all my possessions as food, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy, does not brag, is not puffed up,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not keep count of wrongs,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: does not rejoice over wrongdoing but rejoices together with the truth;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Love never falls. But as for prophecies, they will be done away with; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will be done away with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know in part and we prophesy in part;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but when what is complete comes, what is in part will be done away with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child; when I became a man, I did away with the things of a child.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For now we see by means of a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, just as I have also been fully known.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And now faith, hope, love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a language as well as for the organ of speech; a first-century reader would have heard ‘the languages of people and of angels’. The traditional ‘tongues’ is kept because it is the established name for the gift of speech discussed in chapters 12 to 14.

The Greek names the metal, not an instrument, and literally says ‘echoing bronze’. Most modern versions take it as a gong. Some scholars think it refers to the bronze resonating vessels used to amplify sound in theatres, which make noise but say nothing. The reference is uncertain, so the rendering stays with what the Greek states.

The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter: ‘so that I may be burned’ and ‘so that I may boast’. The SBL text translated here reads ‘be burned’. Several of the earliest manuscripts read ‘boast’, which the Nestle-Aland edition and a number of recent translations adopt. Scholars remain divided.

The verb means to act in a way that is disgraceful or indecent by the standards of an honour-conscious society, which is stronger than bad manners. Paul uses the same word group for dishonourable conduct elsewhere in this letter. ‘Is not rude’ is the common modern rendering and is not wrong, only weaker.

notes.phrase: does not keep count of wrongs
notes.traditional: thinks no evil; keeps no record of wrongs
notes.note: The verb is a bookkeeping term, to reckon or enter in an account, and the object is literally ‘the evil’. Most scholars take this to mean that love does not keep a tally of injuries done to it. The phrase can also mean ‘does not plot evil’, a sense it has in the Greek Old Testament, and older versions rendered it ‘thinks no evil’.

The verb can mean either ‘endure, put up with’ or ‘cover, keep confidential’, so the clause may say that love covers everything in silence and does not expose others’ faults. ‘Bears’ follows Paul’s use of the verb elsewhere for enduring hardship. The fourfold ‘all things’ may also be adverbial, ‘in everything’ or ‘always’, which avoids the suggestion that love is gullible.

notes.traditional: Love never fails; Love never ends
notes.note: The verb is the ordinary word for falling, used figuratively of something collapsing or ceasing to stand. ‘Never fails’ can suggest to a modern reader that love always succeeds. The point is that love, unlike prophecy, tongues and knowledge, never comes to an end.

notes.phrase: they will be done away with
notes.traditional: will fail / vanish away / pass away; put away (v. 11)
notes.note: Paul uses the same verb four times in verses 8 to 11: of prophecies, of knowledge, of what is partial, and of an adult leaving childish ways behind. It means to bring to an end or put out of use. Many translations vary the English; one rendering is used here throughout so that the repetition can be heard.

notes.traditional: that which is perfect; the perfect
notes.note: The adjective means complete, whole or fully grown, and here it stands opposite ‘what is in part’. ‘Complete’ therefore states the contrast more exactly than ‘perfect’, which suggests moral flawlessness. Most scholars take the reference to be the consummation at Christ’s return, when partial knowledge gives way to seeing ‘face to face’ (verse 12).

notes.phrase: by means of a mirror, in a riddle
notes.traditional: through a glass, darkly; in a mirror dimly
notes.note: The Greek says literally ‘through a mirror, in a riddle’. Ancient mirrors were polished metal, and the point is probably that one sees only a reflection and not the thing itself. ‘In a riddle’ echoes Numbers 12:8 in the Greek Old Testament, where God speaks with Moses mouth to mouth and ‘not through riddles’. ‘Dimly’ and ‘darkly’ are interpretive paraphrases of that phrase.

The opening words can be temporal (‘in the present time’) or logical (‘as things stand’, ‘in fact’). On the first reading faith and hope belong to the present age and love alone lasts beyond it. On the second all three remain, in contrast to the gifts that pass away, and love is still the greatest. Interpreters are divided.

candidates.reason: For the speech gift in Acts and 1 Corinthians 12–14, translators split between the traditional ‘tongues’ and ‘languages’, and the choice must be the same in every chapter.
A favourite Pauline verb rendered variously as abolish, nullify, bring to nothing, set aside or pass away; inconsistent English hides its repetition within and across letters.
It recurs in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, where ‘perfect’, ‘mature’ and ‘complete’ all compete and ‘perfect’ often misleads.
In Paul and the Gospels it means a divine secret now disclosed, not a puzzle, so ‘mystery’ versus ‘secret’ needs one decision.
Its accounting sense (reckon, credit, count) is central in Romans 4 and elsewhere, and needs a consistent rendering distinct from its sense of thinking or considering.
